transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Evelyn (CTO - Celestis), Marco (ML Eng), Sara (Infra)

Summary (auto): POC to validate capacity sizing and autoscale behavior for Celestis' real-time summarization and search augmentation workloads. Focus on reserved baseline for predictable latency and burst capacity for peaks.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intro and then dive into capacity and autoscale specifics for the POC.
[00:10] Evelyn: thanks, Maya. we wanna make sure this pilot shows predictable p99 latency under our peak and we don't blow budget.
[00:18] Jonah: yep, totally. quick question on workloads, are you mostly real-time chat/summarization or batch embeddings?
[00:24] Marco: mostly real-time summarization and a small routing layer that does embeddings for rerank on user queries. maybe 70% real-time short queries, 30% async batch embeddings.
[00:34] Sara: infra wise we run in GCP and have a VPC peering option; security will need SOC2 docs, and we may want a private deployment later.
[00:45] Maya: perfect, that's helpful. so for the POC we usually recommend a reserved baseline of GPUs to cover steady-state concurrency, plus burst capacity for peaks. we'll size baseline based on qps and model choice.
[00:58] Jonah: can you share rough numbers for concurrency and payloads? token sizes?
[01:05] Marco: yeah typical request is 80-150 input tokens and output 30-100 tokens. average payload ~200 tokens roundtrip. concurrency at steady state about 25 rps, peaks up to 200 rps for 10-15 min windows.
[01:24] Jonah: ok that helps. so at a high level for a 13B-ish model quantized to int8 we see ~60-80 tokens/sec per GPU for generation depending on batch and seq len, so baseline reserved pool to handle 25 rps with 200 tokens per req is roughly X, we'll do the math live.
[01:40] Marco: ehrm, can you walk through the math? we need the explicit numbers for our budgeting.
[01:45] Jonah: sure — rough calc: if each request is 200 tokens total and a single GPU can do 80 tokens/sec, one GPU handles 0.4 requests/sec (80/200) so to handle 25 rps steady state you'd need ~62 GPU equivalents — that is not realistic for this size so we then leverage batching and smaller model variants for lower latency path. our inference engine does batching which increases tokens/sec significantly for similar latency SLOs. with batching and sequence-aware scheduling we commonly get effective throughput of 3-4 req/sec per GPU for this request shape with optimized kernels.
[02:20] Evelyn: that swing is big — 0.4 to 3-4 — what's the variance? how confident can we be in Pilot?
[02:27] Jonah: good question. variance depends on request size distribution and ability to batch. if your traffic is spiky with single user single tokens we can't batch much. for Celestis' mix (70% short requests) we expect decent batching. for the POC we'll run staged benchmarks with your real traces to get an empirical tokens/sec and QPS per GPU.
[02:43] Sara: for reserved baseline we want a predictable small number to lock budget and then burst on demand. does Redwood offer burst that uses shared capacity or do we pay spot GPUs?
[02:52] Maya: we support both approaches in Redwood Dedicated and Hosted combos: you can reserve a fixed pool (DR) for baseline and then configure burst to Redwood shared fleet which is cheaper but not SLA-backed, or enable dedicated burst using on-demand reserved GPUs in your account in Dedicated. for Pilot usually customers use reserved baseline + Redwood shared burst to prove correctness then move to dedicated burst if they need SLA.
[03:18] Marco: fallback policies — if shared burst is exhausted what's the fallback? we can't have 10s of seconds of tail latency.
[03:24] Jonah: we provide multi-level fallback: first fallback to smaller model variant (e.g., 13B -> quantized 7B or 3B distilled) with graceful degradation; second fallback is region-level routing (route to secondary region) if capacity is regional; third is queueing with a short TTL and immediate consistent response explaining degraded mode. you can configure prioritization so critical users never get downgraded.
[03:46] Evelyn: what's the impact on quality when switching to smaller variants — do you have eval metrics?
[03:50] Maya: we include quality deltas in our Model Catalog and we'll run pairwise evals against your in-house prompts in the POC. Jonah will run hallucination/regression checks in the benchmark harness.
[03:59] Marco: timeline: how long for the POC? we were thinking 6 weeks.
[04:03] Maya: 4-6 weeks is typical: week 0 onboarding + infra setup, week 1-2 benchmark and tuning, week 3 pilot traffic ramp, week 4 wrap and handoff. extendable.
[04:12] Sara: for onboarding we'll need SSO,SAML and KMS integration docs. can you push the SOC2 and architecture whitepaper?
[04:18] Maya: yes will send SOC2, ISO certs, and our private deployment architecture note. expect that in the next email.
[04:25] Jonah: ok circle back to sizing — another lever is KV cache/prefix cache for long context reuse. if your workload often repeats contexts we can cache kvs and reduce per-token compute. do you have reuse patterns?
[04:37] Marco: yes about 30% of requests share same-ish prefix (user profile + app state) so caching could be helpful.
[04:42] Jonah: good — that will reduce steady cpu/gpu demand. we'll include caching-aware benchmarks.
[04:47] Maya: on pricing and POC quote: we'll propose 2 baseline reserved A100-equivalent GPUs for common tests plus a configurable burst policy to the shared fleet. that baseline is conservative but we'll tune after benchmarks.
[04:59] Evelyn: two GPUs sounds low based on earlier math, is that just for initial smoke?
[05:03] Jonah: yes it's an initial smoke and to validate integration, not to emulate production-scale QPS. we typically run staged scale tests using the shared fleet and then size the reserved commit for production. for budgeting you'll get options: small baseline + more burst vs higher baseline and less burst — tradeoff between unit cost predictability and latency SLO.
[05:24] Marco: what about autoscaling triggers — latency based or queue length? what's recommended for POC?
[05:29] Jonah: recommended approach: hybrid triggers — scale up on p95/p99 latency breach or sustained queue length above threshold for X seconds. also scale-down with conservative cooldowns to avoid flapping. for POC we'll test a few policies.
[05:42] Sara: and scale window — minutes to spin up a new GPU instance is a concern. how fast is cold-start?
[05:49] Jonah: cold-start to provision a dedicated GPU can be 2-6 minutes depending on infra. to mitigate we use warm standby GPUs and prewarmed model caches. for the shared fleet cold-start is shorter because infra is pooled but you still pay a slightly higher unit. you can also use preloaded checkpoints in KV cache to reduce warm time.
[06:06] Evelyn: can we set hard fallbacks so if scale can't happen we failover to the smaller model instead of queueing?
[06:11] Jonah: yes that's configurable; you can set priority rules: attempt to scale, if unsuccessful within threshold then return degraded model; or for critical routes never degrade and queue instead.
[06:21] Maya: question about benchmarks: Jonah will run a suite — p50,p95,p99 latencies, throughput, tokens/sec, memory pressure, GPU util, and cost per 1M tokens. we'll run for short burst profiles and steady traffic.
[06:36] Marco: please include an A/B between int8 quant and fp16 for our model. we care about quality delta.
[06:41] Jonah: will do — int8 vs fp16 eval + qualitative samples and automated eval scripts.
[06:46] Sara: security: audit logs, key rotation, KMS/HSM support — can you confirm log retention windows?
[06:52] Maya: we support configurable audit log retention; for Private customers we can match your retention policy; for Hosted we provide up to 13 months by default and extended retention as add-on. KMS integrations supported for Private and Dedicated.
[07:05] Evelyn: governance — we need RBAC and SSO for pilots.
[07:08] Maya: RBAC and SAML SSO are available, we'll include the SAML metadata in the onboarding doc.
[07:14] Marco: one more on fallback policies — when you downgrade to smaller model, do you keep the same prompt or you alter the prompt to compensate?
[07:20] Jonah: good ops detail — we can optionally re-prompt or use a condensed system prompt for smaller models. commonly we send a shorter context and an explicit note to the model to be concise; we'll include prompt management in the harness.
[07:33] Evelyn: benchmarks — can you run them on our staging VPC? we prefer staging to match network latency.
[07:37] Maya: yes staging VPC pegged to your account is preferred for fidelity. Jonah will need access and sample traces.
[07:44] Jonah: for the test harness I'll share a repo link and a checklist: throughput, spike test, traffic recency, tail-latency profile, cache-hit ratio, model-switch regression tests.
[07:55] Maya: budget guardrails — for POC we'll include cost caps on burst, and alerts if expected spend exceeds threshold.
[07:59] Sara: that helps. what about regional failover — do you replicate models across regions ahead of time?
[08:05] Jonah: replication is optional; we can pre-stage smaller model variants in secondary region to enable fast failover. full-size models we can warm in advance if you want cross-region SLO.
[08:15] Marco: metrics and dashboards — can Redwood surface token-level cost and per-route latency?
[08:19] Maya: yes Redwood Console shows token-level cost breakdowns, per-route/model dashboards, and tracing hooks. We'll add access to a demo workspace for Celestis.
[08:29] Evelyn: ok im starting to feel comfortable. concrete POC deliverables?
[08:33] Maya: deliverables: 1) benchmark report with sizing recommendations and cost projections 2) autoscale and fallback policy config we tested 3) integration checklist + runbook 4) quality regression results between model variants.
[08:46] Marco: and acceptance criteria?
[08:48] Maya: acceptance: p99 latency under 800ms for critical routes under expected peak traffic with <5% error/regression versus baseline quality. if not met we'll iterate.
[08:58] Sara: timeline and dates recap?
[09:01] Maya: Jonah to share harness (due 12/14), Maya to send pricing (due 12/15), Celestis to provide traces (due 12/16). staging benchmark week of 12/20. follow-up sync 12/22 to review results and sizing.
[09:14] Evelyn: ok thanks, one more quick question — for billing during POC how is burst charged?
[09:20] Maya: burst on shared fleet is usage-based hourly equivalent at lower unit price but not reserved; if you use Dedicated burst in your account it's billed at standard cloud rates or reserved rates you commit to. we'll show both scenarios in the quote.
[09:34] Marco: small nit: when you show the model variants list please include expected memory footprints so we can plan for instance types.
[09:40] Jonah: will include memory and GPU-memory usage estimates per model and quantization format.
[09:45] Maya: any other blockers?
[09:47] Sara: just ensuring legal has the onboarding timeline; we'll route SOC2 and DPA review internally.
[09:52] Maya: ok noted.
[09:54] Jonah: FYI we'll also test fallback latency — switching to smaller variant should add <150ms extra in our tests when prewarmed; cold-switch may be higher.
[10:03] Evelyn: great. can you send the checklist now?
[10:05] Jonah: yes sharing after call.
[10:07] Maya: recap of next steps and then we'll close.
[10:09] Maya: recap: Jonah share harness (12/14), Maya send pricing + POC quote (12/15), Celestis provide logs (12/16), staging run week of 12/20, follow-up 12/22. action items in email.
[10:21] Marco: sounds good. thanks all.
[10:24] Evelyn: thanks. bye.
